# Part A: Walkthrough

## 1. The model

Week 1 assumed that an infected host is infectious immediately. The SEIR model
relaxes that: a newly infected host first enters an **exposed** class $E$
(infected, not yet infectious) and moves on to $I$ at rate $\sigma$, so that
$1/\sigma$ is the mean latent period. With birth and death rate $\mu$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S' &= \mu - \beta I S - \mu S, \\
E' &= \beta I S - (\sigma+\mu)E, \\
I' &= \sigma E - (\gamma+\mu)I, \\
R' &= \gamma I - \mu R.
\end{aligned}
$$

In code, the model is a function that takes the current state and returns the
four derivatives. This is the form `deSolve` expects.

```{r model}
seir <- function(t, y, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(y, parms)), {
    dS <- mu - beta * I * S - mu * S
    dE <- beta * I * S - (sigma + mu) * E
    dI <- sigma * E - (gamma + mu) * I
    dR <- gamma * I - mu * R
    list(c(dS, dE, dI, dR))
  })
}
```

Our running example is a flu-like infection: a latent period of 3 days, an
infectious period of 5 days, and a life expectancy of 70 years.

```{r parameters}
parms <- c(beta  = 0.6,            # transmission coefficient, per day
           sigma = 1 / 3,          # 1 / latent period
           gamma = 1 / 5,          # 1 / infectious period
           mu    = 1 / (70 * 365)) # 1 / life expectancy
```

A small helper runs the solver and returns a data frame. The tight tolerances
matter later, when $I$ becomes very small.

```{r solver}
run_seir <- function(parms, y0, times) {
  as.data.frame(ode(y = y0, times = times, func = seir, parms = parms,
                    rtol = 1e-8, atol = 1e-12))
}

y0    <- c(S = 1 - 1e-6, E = 0, I = 1e-6, R = 0)   # one infectious host per million
times <- seq(0, 200, by = 0.5)
out   <- run_seir(parms, y0, times)
head(out)
```

```{r first-plot}
to_long <- function(out, vars = c("S", "E", "I", "R")) {
  data.frame(time        = rep(out$time, length(vars)),
             compartment = factor(rep(vars, each = nrow(out)), levels = vars),
             fraction    = unlist(out[vars], use.names = FALSE))
}

ggplot(to_long(out), aes(time, fraction, colour = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "time (days)", y = "fraction of the population",
       title = "One SEIR epidemic")
```

The $E$ curve rises first and the $I$ curve follows it: every infectious host
was exposed a few days earlier.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. What the latent period changes, and what it does not

The notes derive

$$
R_0 = \beta\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\sigma+\mu}\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma+\mu}
    = \frac{\beta\sigma}{(\sigma+\mu)(\gamma+\mu)} .
$$

The latent period enters only through $\sigma/(\sigma+\mu)$, the probability
of surviving latency, which is essentially $1$ when the latent period is days
and a lifetime is decades.

```{r R0-formula}
R0_formula <- function(parms) {
  with(as.list(parms), beta * sigma / ((sigma + mu) * (gamma + mu)))
}
R0_formula(parms)
```

So changing the latent period should leave $R_0$ almost untouched. Here are
three latent periods, everything else fixed.

```{r latent-sweep}
latent_days <- c(0.5, 3, 8)

runs <- lapply(latent_days, function(L) {
  p <- parms
  p["sigma"] <- 1 / L
  d <- run_seir(p, y0, seq(0, 300, by = 0.5))
  d$latent <- paste(L, "days")
  d$R0 <- R0_formula(p)
  d
})
runs <- do.call(rbind, runs)
runs$latent <- factor(runs$latent, levels = paste(latent_days, "days"))

ggplot(runs, aes(time, I, colour = latent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "time (days)", y = "I(t)", colour = "latent period",
       title = "Same R0, different clocks")
```

```{r latent-table}
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(runs, runs$latent), function(d) {
  data.frame(latent_period = d$latent[1],
             R0            = round(d$R0[1], 4),
             peak_day      = d$time[which.max(d$I)],
             peak_I        = round(max(d$I), 4),
             lowest_S      = round(min(d$S), 3))
}))
```

$R_0$ differs by less than one part in a thousand across the three runs, and
the lowest value $S$ reaches, a measure of how much of the population the
epidemic infects, is close in all three. (The small differences come from
births, which keep adding susceptibles while the slower epidemics run.
Question 2 of the homework removes births and makes the statement exact.) What
changes is *when* the epidemic happens, and how tall its peak is.

### How fast does it grow?

Early in an epidemic $S\approx 1$, and the infected compartments obey the
linearization at the disease-free equilibrium. The notes show that, apart
from the eigenvalue $\Lambda_1=-\mu$, the eigenvalues $\Lambda$ of $J(P_0)$ are
the roots of

$$
\Lambda^2+(\sigma+\gamma+2\mu)\,\Lambda+(\sigma+\mu)(\gamma+\mu)(1-R_0)=0 .
$$

When $R_0>1$ its roots have opposite signs. The positive root, call it $r$, is
the **early exponential growth rate**: $I(t)$ grows like $e^{rt}$.

```{r growth-rate}
growth_rate <- function(parms) {
  with(as.list(parms), {
    b  <- sigma + gamma + 2 * mu
    c0 <- (sigma + mu) * (gamma + mu) * (1 - R0_formula(parms))
    (-b + sqrt(b^2 - 4 * c0)) / 2
  })
}
r_predicted <- growth_rate(parms)
r_predicted
```

That is a prediction from a matrix. We can test it against the simulation by
fitting a straight line to $\log I(t)$ over the early part of the epidemic.

```{r growth-fit}
t_peak <- out$time[which.max(out$I)]
early  <- subset(out, time < t_peak & I > 1e-5 & I < 1e-3)
fit    <- lm(log(I) ~ time, data = early)

c(predicted = r_predicted, fitted = unname(coef(fit)["time"]))
```

```{r growth-plot}
ggplot(out, aes(time, I)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit)[1] / log(10), slope = r_predicted / log(10),
              linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "time (days)", y = "I(t), log scale",
       title = "Early growth is exponential, at the rate the Jacobian predicts",
       subtitle = "dashed: a line with slope r")
```

For comparison, the SIR model with the same $\beta$ and $\gamma$ grows at rate
$\beta-(\gamma+\mu)$:

```{r growth-sir}
c(SEIR = r_predicted,
  SIR  = unname(parms["beta"] - (parms["gamma"] + parms["mu"])))
```

The two models have almost the same $R_0$, but the SEIR epidemic grows at less
than half the speed. **$R_0$ counts infections per generation; it says nothing
about how long a generation takes.** Question 6 of the homework turns this
around.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Equilibria

Setting the right-hand sides to zero gives the disease-free equilibrium
$P_0=(1,0,0)$ and, when $R_0>1$, the endemic equilibrium

$$
S^*=\frac{1}{R_0},\qquad I^*=\frac{\mu}{\beta}(R_0-1),\qquad E^*=\frac{\gamma+\mu}{\sigma}\,I^* .
$$

```{r equilibrium}
endemic_eq <- function(parms) {
  with(as.list(parms), {
    R0     <- R0_formula(parms)
    S_star <- 1 / R0
    I_star <- mu / beta * (R0 - 1)
    E_star <- (gamma + mu) / sigma * I_star
    c(S = S_star, E = E_star, I = I_star, R = 1 - S_star - E_star - I_star)
  })
}
P_star <- endemic_eq(parms)
P_star
```

A formula for an equilibrium is easy to check: plug it into the model and the
derivatives should all be zero.

```{r equilibrium-check}
seir(0, P_star, parms)[[1]]
```

Notice how small $I^*$ is. At the endemic equilibrium about a third of the
population is susceptible, but only about one person in ten thousand is
infectious at any moment.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. The next-generation matrix

The general recipe: take the infected compartments only, $x=(E,I)$, and write
$x'=\mathcal{F}-\mathcal{V}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ holds the **new infections**
and $\mathcal{V}$ holds every other transfer. For SEIR,

$$
\mathcal{F}=\begin{pmatrix}\beta I S\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathcal{V}=\begin{pmatrix}(\sigma+\mu)E\\ (\gamma+\mu)I-\sigma E\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $(E,I)$ at the disease-free equilibrium
$(S,E,I)=(1,0,0)$ gives

$$
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
V=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma+\mu&0\\-\sigma&\gamma+\mu\end{pmatrix},
$$

and then $K=FV^{-1}$ and $R_0=\rho(K)$, the largest eigenvalue of $K$ in
absolute value.

```{r ngm}
ngm <- function(parms) {
  with(as.list(parms), {
    nm   <- list(c("E", "I"), c("E", "I"))
    Fmat <- matrix(c(0, beta,
                     0, 0), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = nm)
    Vmat <- matrix(c(sigma + mu, 0,
                     -sigma,     gamma + mu), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = nm)
    Vinv <- solve(Vmat)          # matrix inverse
    K    <- Fmat %*% Vinv        # matrix product
    list(F = Fmat, V = Vmat, Vinv = Vinv, K = K,
         R0 = max(Mod(eigen(K)$values)))
  })
}
res <- ngm(parms)
res$F
res$V
```

$V^{-1}$ has a meaning of its own. Entry $(i,j)$ is the expected time that a
host starting in compartment $j$ (column) spends in compartment $i$ (row).

```{r ngm-vinv}
res$Vinv
```

Read the first column: a host entering $E$ spends about 3 days there and
then, on average, about 5 days in $I$. Read the second column: a host placed
directly in $I$ spends about 5 days there and never visits $E$.

Multiplying by $F$ turns time spent into new infections produced:

```{r ngm-K}
res$K
eigen(res$K)$values
c(from_matrix = res$R0, from_formula = R0_formula(parms))
```

The matrix method and the formula agree. The bottom row of $K$ is zero because
every new infection enters $E$; none enters $I$ directly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Local stability

The Jacobian of the reduced system, in the order $(S,E,I)$, is

$$
J(S,E,I)=\begin{pmatrix}
-\beta I-\mu & 0 & -\beta S\\
\beta I & -(\sigma+\mu) & \beta S\\
0 & \sigma & -(\gamma+\mu)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

```{r jacobian}
jacobian <- function(state, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parms)), {
    matrix(c(-beta * I - mu,  0,              -beta * S,
              beta * I,       -(sigma + mu),   beta * S,
              0,               sigma,         -(gamma + mu)),
           nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  })
}
P_0 <- c(S = 1, E = 0, I = 0)

eigen(jacobian(P_0, parms))$values
eigen(jacobian(P_star, parms))$values
```

At $P_0$ one eigenvalue is positive, so $P_0$ is unstable. That positive
eigenvalue is exactly the growth rate $r$ from Section 2. At $P^*$ all three
real parts are negative, so $P^*$ is asymptotically stable, as the theorem in
the notes says it must be when $R_0>1$.

The notes prove the $P^*$ case through the Routh--Hurwitz conditions:
$\operatorname{tr}J<0$, $\det J<0$, and $\operatorname{tr}J\cdot a_2-\det J<0$,
where $a_2$ is the sum of the three $2\times 2$ principal minors.

```{r routh-hurwitz}
J  <- jacobian(P_star, parms)
tr <- sum(diag(J))
a2 <- det(J[c(1, 2), c(1, 2)]) + det(J[c(1, 3), c(1, 3)]) + det(J[c(2, 3), c(2, 3)])
c(trace = tr, a2 = a2, det = det(J), third_condition = tr * a2 - det(J))
```

One set of parameters is an example, not a proof. But we can at least watch
the theorem hold across a whole range of $\beta$, passing through $R_0=1$.

```{r stability-sweep}
beta_grid <- seq(0.05, 1.2, length.out = 200)

sweep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(beta_grid, function(b) {
  p <- parms
  p["beta"] <- b
  R0 <- R0_formula(p)
  at_P0    <- max(Re(eigen(jacobian(P_0, p))$values))
  at_Pstar <- if (R0 > 1) max(Re(eigen(jacobian(endemic_eq(p), p))$values)) else NA
  data.frame(R0 = R0,
             equilibrium = c("P0 (disease-free)", "P* (endemic)"),
             leading = c(at_P0, at_Pstar))
}))
sweep <- na.omit(sweep)

ggplot(sweep, aes(R0, leading)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ equilibrium, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = expression(R[0]), y = "largest real part of the eigenvalues",
       title = "Stability changes hands at R0 = 1")
```

In the left panel the curve crosses zero exactly at $R_0=1$: $P_0$ is stable
below the threshold and unstable above it. In the right panel the curve stays
below zero wherever $P^*$ exists. Look at the vertical scales, though. At $P^*$
the leading real part is thousands of times smaller than at $P_0$. The endemic
equilibrium is stable, but only weakly: the return to it is very slow.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. The slow approach to the endemic equilibrium

To see that slow return, start near $P^*$ with twice the endemic level of
infection, and run for 150 years.

```{r long-run}
y_near <- c(S = P_star[["S"]], E = 2 * P_star[["E"]], I = 2 * P_star[["I"]])
y_near <- c(y_near, R = 1 - sum(y_near))

long_run <- run_seir(parms, y_near, seq(0, 150 * 365, by = 5))

ggplot(long_run, aes(time / 365, I)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = P_star[["I"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "time (years)", y = "I(t)",
       title = "Damped oscillations toward the endemic equilibrium",
       subtitle = "dashed: I*")
```

The eigenvalues of $J(P^*)$ explain both features of this picture. A complex
pair $a\pm ib$ produces oscillations with period $2\pi/b$ inside an envelope
$e^{at}$. Keeling and Rohani give the approximation $T\approx 2\pi\sqrt{AG}$,
with $A=1/(\mu(R_0-1))$ the mean age at infection and
$G=\frac{1}{\gamma+\mu}+\frac{1}{\sigma+\mu}$ the generation time.

```{r period}
ev <- eigen(jacobian(P_star, parms))$values
ev

A <- 1 / (parms[["mu"]] * (R0_formula(parms) - 1))
G <- 1 / (parms[["gamma"]] + parms[["mu"]]) + 1 / (parms[["sigma"]] + parms[["mu"]])

# locate the peaks of the simulated I(t) and average the gaps between them
peaks <- which(diff(sign(diff(long_run$I))) == -2) + 1

c(period_from_eigenvalue  = 2 * pi / max(Im(ev)) / 365,
  period_Keeling_Rohani   = 2 * pi * sqrt(A * G) / 365,
  period_from_simulation  = mean(diff(long_run$time[peaks])) / 365,
  damping_time            = 1 / abs(Re(ev[which.max(Im(ev))])) / 365)
```

All four numbers are in years. Compare the three independent routes to the
period: the eigenvalues, the approximation, and simply measuring the
simulation. The damping time is the time for the oscillation's amplitude to fall
by a factor of $e$.

Compare the two clocks in this model: an epidemic is over in a few months
(Section 1), while the approach to endemic equilibrium takes generations.

Answer every part in this document. For the math parts, write your derivation
under **Your answer** using LaTeX, showing the steps and not only the result.
For the code parts, use the empty chunk. Reuse the functions defined in Part A
(`seir`, `run_seir`, `R0_formula`, `ngm`, `jacobian`, `endemic_eq`); copy and
modify them when a question changes the model. Questions 1--6 are required;

## Before you start: the diseases behind these models

Each model in this homework is a simplification that fits some real infections
well. What decides the choice is the biology: whether infected people recover,
whether recovery leaves them immune, and whether there is a delay between
being infected and being able to infect others.

| Model | Main assumption | Typical diseases |
|:--|:--|:--|
| SI | Infected people never recover. | HIV without treatment: infection is lifelong. |
| SIS | Recovery gives no immunity, so recovered people are immediately susceptible again. | Gonorrhea and chlamydia: antibiotics cure the infection but leave no protection against catching it again. |
| SIR, closed population | Recovery gives lifelong immunity, and the outbreak is short compared with a human lifetime. | A single outbreak in a closed group, such as the classic 1978 influenza outbreak in an English boarding school, where 512 of 763 boys fell ill in about two weeks. |
| SIR with births and deaths | Lifelong immunity; births supply new susceptibles, so the infection can persist for decades. | Measles, chickenpox, and mumps before vaccination, which returned every year or every few years in large cities. |
| SEIR | As SIR, plus a latent period: infected but not yet infectious. | Measles (about ten days from infection to becoming infectious), chickenpox, and COVID-19 (a few days). |
| SEIR with vaccination at birth (Question 3) | A fraction of newborns is immune from the start. | Measles, mumps, and rubella (the MMR vaccine), and polio, all part of routine childhood vaccination. |
| SEIAR, with an asymptomatic class (Question 7) | Some infected people never develop symptoms but can still transmit. | Polio (about 7 in 10 infections cause no symptoms), COVID-19, influenza, and cholera. |

These are the textbook matches, not exact descriptions. Real diseases mix
features: immunity to influenza fades as the virus changes, and some
hepatitis B infections become chronic rather than ending in recovery. The
class app includes four more models (waning immunity, disease deaths,
isolation of cases, and chronic carriers), each with its typical diseases on
its first tab.

## Question 1. Warm-up: the models you already know

The next-generation matrix is not only for models with several infected
compartments. When there is a single infected compartment, $x=(I)$, the
"matrices" $F$ and $V$ are $1\times 1$, that is, plain numbers, and
$K=FV^{-1}=F/V$. Each model below is written in the notation in which you
first met it: the first, third, and fourth in absolute numbers, the second in
proportions.

1. **Closed SIR** (Week 1): $S'=-\beta IS$, $\ I'=\beta IS-\gamma I$, $\ R'=\gamma I$, with $S(0)=S_0$.
2. **SIR with demography** (Week 1): $S'=\mu-\beta IS-\mu S$, $\ I'=\beta IS-(\gamma+\mu)I$, $\ R'=\gamma I-\mu R$.
3. **SIS** (Week 2): $S'=-\beta IS+\gamma I$, $\ I'=\beta IS-\gamma I$, with $S+I=N_0$.
4. **SI** (no recovery): $S'=-\beta IS$, $\ I'=\beta IS$, with $S(0)=S_0$.

**(a) Math.** For each model, state the disease-free equilibrium you are
linearizing at, split the $I$ equation into $\mathcal{F}$ (new infections) and
$\mathcal{V}$ (everything else), and compute $F$, $V$, and $R_0=F/V$. Show the
work for each model, then summarize it in the table. For models 1--3, confirm
that you recover exactly the threshold quantity from Weeks 1 and 2.

### Closed SIR

$$
\begin{aligned}
S' &= -\beta IS \\
I' &= \beta IS - \gamma I \\
R' &= \gamma I\\
S(0) &= S_0
\end{aligned}
$$

| Equation | Term | Meaning | Assigned To |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| \(I'\) | \(\beta I S\) | Rate of New Infection | \(F_1 = \beta I S\) |
| \(I'\) | \(-\gamma I\) | Rate of Recovery | \(V_1 = \gamma I\) |

$$
\mathcal{F} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\mathcal{V} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma
\end{pmatrix}
,
\mathcal{V}^{-1}=\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)
$$

$$
K = \mathcal{F}\mathcal{V}^{-1}=\frac{\beta}{\gamma}
$$

$$
R_0=\frac{\beta}{\gamma}
$$

---

### SIR with Demography

$$
\begin{aligned}
S' &= \mu-\beta IS-\mu S \\
I' &= \beta IS-(\gamma+\mu)I \\
R' &= \gamma I-\mu R\\
S(0) &= S_0
\end{aligned}
$$

| Equation | Term | Meaning | Assigned To |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| \(I'\) | \(\beta I S\) | Rate of New Infection | \(F_1 = \beta I S\) |
| \(I'\) | \(-(\gamma+\mu)I\) | Rate of Recovery or Death | \(V_1 = (\gamma+\mu)I\) |

$$
\mathcal{F} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\mathcal{V} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma+\mu
\end{pmatrix}
,
\mathcal{V}^{-1}=\left(\frac{1}{\gamma+\mu}\right)
$$

$$
K=\mathcal{F}\mathcal{V}^{-1}
=\frac{\beta}{\gamma+\mu}
$$

$$
R_0=\frac{\beta}{\gamma+\mu}
$$

---

### SIS

$$
\begin{aligned}
S' &= -\beta IS+\gamma I \\
I' &= \beta IS-\gamma I \\
S+I &= N_0
\end{aligned}
$$

| Equation | Term | Meaning | Assigned To |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| \(I'\) | \(\beta I S\) | Rate of New Infection | \(F_1 = \beta I S\) |
| \(I'\) | \(-\gamma I\) | Rate of Recovery | \(V_1 = \gamma I\) |

$$
\mathcal{F} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\mathcal{V} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma
\end{pmatrix}
,
\mathcal{V}^{-1}=\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)
$$

$$
K=\mathcal{F}\mathcal{V}^{-1}
=\frac{\beta}{\gamma}
$$

$$
R_0=\frac{\beta}{\gamma}
$$

---

### SI

$$
\begin{aligned}
S' &= -\beta IS \\
I' &= \beta IS \\
S(0) &= S_0
\end{aligned}
$$

| Equation | Term | Meaning | Assigned To |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| \(I'\) | \(\beta I S\) | Rate of New Infection | \(F_1 = \beta I S\) |
| \(I'\) | Nothing | There is no recovery | \(V_1 = 0\) |

$$
\mathcal{F} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
R_0=\beta
$$

| Model | Disease-free equilibrium | \(F\) | \(V\) | \(R_0\) |
|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
| Closed SIR | (1, 0, 0) | \(\beta\) | \(\gamma\) | \(\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\) |
| SIR with demography | (1, 0, 0) | \(\beta\) | \(\gamma+\mu\) | \(\frac{\beta}{\gamma+\mu}\) |
| SIS | (1, 0) | \(\beta\) | \(\gamma\) | \(\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\) |
| SI | (1, 0) | \(\beta\) | 0 | Undefined |

**(b) Math.** In the SIS model, recovered hosts return to $S$; in the SIR
models they do not. Why does that difference not show up in $R_0$?

$R_0$ concerns itself with the rate at which infected enter and leave the infected category. At the disease free equilibrium, $S = S_0$. That means that it doesn't really matter if the infected return to susceptible or become immune.

**(c) Math.** What goes wrong with the method for the SI model? Say what the
failure means biologically. Then suppose infected hosts die at rate $\alpha$,
so that $I'=\beta IS-\alpha I$, and recompute $R_0$.

Because there is no recovery, `V` is zero. That means `R0` encounters division by zero.

$$
\mathcal{F} = (\beta)
$$

$$
\mathcal{V} = (\alpha)
$$

$$
\mathcal{V}^{-1} = \frac{1}{\alpha}
$$

$$
K = \mathcal{F}\mathcal{V}^{-1}
  = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}
$$

$$
R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}
$$

**(d) Code.** Write a function `R0_from_FV(Fmat, Vmat)` that takes any two
square matrices and returns $\rho(FV^{-1})$. Test it on the four models above
(a $1\times 1$ matrix is `matrix(x, 1, 1)`), using $\beta=0.6$,
$\gamma=0.2$, $\mu$ as in Part A, and $S_0=N_0=1$, and then on the SEIR
matrices from Section 4, where it should agree with `ngm(parms)$R0`. Report
what R does when you give it the SI model. (This chunk is set up so that an
error message is printed in your knitted document and does not stop the
knit.) You will reuse this function in the later questions.

```{r hw1, error=TRUE}
R0_from_FV <- function(Fmat,Vmat)
{
  Vinv <- solve(Vmat)
  K <- Fmat %*% Vinv
  evalues <- eigen(K)
  r0 <- max(evalues$values)
  return(r0)
}

beta <- 0.6
gamma <- 0.2
mu <- 1 / (70 * 365)
sigma = 1 / 3

#SIR 
F <- matrix(c(beta), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
V <- matrix(c(gamma), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
print(R0_from_FV(F, V))

#SIR Demography
F <- matrix(c(beta), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
V <- matrix(c(gamma + mu), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
print(R0_from_FV(F, V))
#SIS
F <- matrix(c(beta), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
V <- matrix(c(gamma), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
print(R0_from_FV(F, V))
#SIER
F <- matrix(c(0, beta, 0, 0), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
V <- matrix(c(sigma+mu, 0, -sigma, gamma+mu), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
print(R0_from_FV(F, V))
#SI
F <- matrix(c(beta), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
V <- matrix(c(0), nrow = 1, ncol = 1)
print(R0_from_FV(F, V))

```
